h: Birds, bay and a bit of caution
p: Morecambe Bay is one of the most important places in Britain for birds, and the jetty is a cracking spot to see them. In autumn and winter especially, huge flocks of wading birds gather on the sands, with oystercatchers, curlews and knot among them. You don't need to be an expert to enjoy the sight of thousands of birds swirling over the water as the tide moves, so bring binoculars if you've got them.

The jetty's public art takes its lead from those birds. Keep an eye out for the bird-themed sculptures and designs along the way; they're part of an art project celebrating the bay's wildlife, and they're great fun to spot with children. At the end of the jetty you'll find the little lighthouse and the old station building, a reminder of the days when the harbour was busy with boats and trains.

This is important. Morecambe Bay's sands look inviting, but they're notorious for quicksand and very fast tides, which can come in quicker than you'd ever expect. Stick to the jetty, the promenade and the beach close to the sea wall. The famous cross-bay walks are only done with the official guide, so never try to strike out across the bay on your own.
Make it a full day by heading along the promenade and finishing with tea and a sunset view. Morecambe's sunsets over the bay, with the Lakeland fells behind, are something special.
